title: The ground of our asking (Revelations 41)
hook: Julian hears: I am the ground of your beseeching
tomorrow: a servant runs to obey and lands in a ditch. now what?

segments.voice: Give me yourself: Julian held all that is made like a hazelnut, and asked for the one holding it. Only you suffice. A few chapters on, she hears where prayer itself comes from.

Thirst shows up before any decision. Nobody plans to be thirsty; the body asks first, and then a hand reaches for the glass. A dry throat, a glance at the water bottle, and the hand is already moving. So who starts a prayer? It seems obvious: the person praying. Someone wants something, asks for it, and waits to see whether God answers. The asking comes first; God's part comes after. In chapter forty-one of her book, Julian of Norwich hears that order turned completely around.
screen: `THIRST COMES FIRST.` → `WHO STARTS A PRAYER?` → `THE ORDER, TURNED AROUND.`

segments.voice: Our Lord, she says, showed her this: "I am Ground of thy beseeching." Beseeching is an old word for asking with your whole heart. Then the order of events, as Julian heard it. First, it's God's will that you have the thing. Then God makes you want it. Then God makes you ask for it, and you ask. So how could it be, she's told, that you wouldn't have what you ask for? The prayer you thought was yours started somewhere else. Your asking is the last link in a chain that began with God wanting to give. Like thirst: the wanting arrives before the reaching. Julian draws a few things out of this. Prayer isn't talking a reluctant God into something; the wanting was his first. And when prayer feels like nothing, dry and barren, she hears that it's still very pleasing to God, even when we feel nothing and see nothing. So she's told to pray anyway. Thanks belongs inside prayer too: an inward knowing, turning the whole self, with reverence and joy, toward what God is stirring. Here's the one to tell a friend: Julian doesn't promise that every request turns out the way we pictured. What she gives is the root of it. The asking begins with him.
screen: `I AM GROUND OF THY BESEECHING.` · `HE WILLS IT, STIRS IT, THEN WE ASK.` · `DRY PRAYER STILL PLEASES GOD.` · `THANKS, INSIDE THE ASKING.` · then, large: `HE WANTS YOU TO ASK.`

segments.voice: If there's water nearby, hold the glass a moment before you drink, and notice the thirst that came first. Take one slow sip and feel it land. Without water, notice the breath instead: the body asks for air before you choose to breathe. For the rest of the sit, bring to mind one good thing you deeply want, and wonder whether that wanting, too, started on the other side.
The ground of our asking. Julian's teaching that God is the root of prayer: he wills it, stirs the wanting, and then we ask.
screen: `THE GROUND OF OUR ASKING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: he wants you to ask, because the asking was his idea first. Day sixteen-thirty-five, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Julian of Norwich often take this chapter as encouragement to keep praying in dry seasons, and her line 'I am Ground of thy beseeching' is used in prayer and spiritual direction.

chat.meaning: Julian hears that prayer which feels dry and barren is still very pleasing to God, and that the asking begins with him.

notes: Confirm the Warrack (1901) wording 'I am Ground of thy beseeching' word for word. The sequence (my will that thou have it; I make thee to will it; I make thee to beseech it) and 'how should it then be that thou shouldst not have thy beseeching?' are paraphrased.
Dryness and barrenness ('then is thy prayer full pleasant to me') and the account of thanking ('a true inward knowing… turning ourselves') are paraphrased from chapter 41; confirm.
Senses shape: thirst before drinking carries the idea; the thirst image is the lesson's own, not Julian's.
